newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Albright says Iraq is sabotaging oil-for-food deal.
newsitem.headline: Albright says Iraq is sabotaging oil-for-food deal.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright accused Iraqi President Saddam Hussein on Friday of deliberately holding up a new oil-for-food deal by making "outrageous demands" on U.N. staff assigned to monitor it.
"The fault lies not with the United States but with Saddam Hussein, who is deliberately preventing the coming into effect of 986," she said, referring to the resolution setting up the plan.

Albright, who denied allegations that the Clinton administration was delaying the deal, spoke to reporters after the Security Council, as expected, retained blanket sanctions against Iraq at its regular 60-day review. They were first imposed in August 1990 after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait.

A key condition for any easing of sanctions would be a report by the U.N. Special Commission in charge of eliminating Iraq's weapons of mass destruction saying that Baghdad had disclosed full details of its nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile programmes.

In its last half-yearly report to the Security Council on Oct. 11, the commission said Iraq might still be hiding small but significant quantities of banned arms. But because of the devastating effect of the sanctions on the Iraqi people, the council separately set up an oil-for-food deal that would allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to purchase food, medicine and other supplies.

The agreement, signed in a memorandum of understanding between Iraq and the United Nations in May, was put on hold after Iraqi troops, for the first time since the end of the 1991 Gulf War, entered the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of the country at the end of August to back a Kurdish faction.

Albright said Iraq last month made "outrageous demands contrary to the memorandum that they signed." These included replacing all local staff members the United Nations had hired, cutting its 150-person monitoring staff nearly in half, curtailing monitors' freedom of movement and making Baghdad the beneficiary of a U.N. escrow account set up to receive the oil revenues.

U.N. officials last month rejected these conditions. But they reported that Iraqi Ambassador Nizar Hamdoon had said the controversy could be resolved if the United States did not hold up an oil-pricing mechanism.
The Security Council's sanctions committee has to approve an pricing formula that changes each month based on trading values of oil from a number of regions.

Albright said the oil-pricing controversy was a "phony issue" raised by Iraq and the United States would look at the formulas when Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali determined that the oil-for-food deal could go ahead.
"We are more concerned about the people of Iraq than Saddam Hussein is. The issue here is what is going on on the ground," she said.

Most diplomats prefer to endorse the formula in advance so their oil experts can approve contracts quickly once the deal goes through. In August, when the last pricing formula was presented, only the United States delayed approval.

The committee this week received a new pricing plan, but Albright indicated the issue was academic while Iraq was issuing unacceptable demands. The committee, composed of all 15 members of the Security Council, needs a unanimous vote for its decisions.
